scenarios.title: Introducing yourself
scenarios.description: You are at a class, workshop or community group and would like to say who you are.
scenarios.setting: A class, workshop or community group
conversationStarters: Hi, I'm [name]. I'm fairly new here.
Hello, I don't think we've met. I'm [name].
Hi, I'm [name]. What brought you along today?
followUpQuestions: How did you get into this?
Have you been coming for long?
What do you enjoy most about it?

prompts.heard: Nice to meet you! What do you do?
suggestions: I work in [field]. How about you?
I'm studying [subject]. What about you?
Mostly [short answer]. What brings you here?

prompts.heard: Where are you from?
suggestions: I grew up in [place]. Have you always lived here?
I'm from [place], but I live in [place] now. And you?
Originally [place]. Do you know it?

prompts.heard: Have you been to one of these before?
suggestions: This is my first one. Any tips?
A couple of times. How about you?
Not yet. What's it usually like?

listeningTips: Look at the person while they speak, if that feels comfortable.
Repeat their name once to help you remember it.
A short introduction is perfectly fine.

scenarios.title: Joining a conversation
scenarios.description: A small group is chatting and you would like to join in for a bit.
scenarios.setting: A break room, a party, or a group event
conversationStarters: Mind if I join you?
That sounds interesting. What are you talking about?
Hi, I overheard something about [topic]. I like that too.
followUpQuestions: What did you think of it?
How did you hear about it?
What would you recommend?

prompts.heard: Sure, come on in! We were talking about weekend plans.
suggestions: Thanks! I'm still deciding mine. What are you up to?
Sounds good. Anyone doing anything fun?
I'll just listen for a moment, if that's okay.

prompts.heard: Have you seen that new show everyone's talking about?
suggestions: Not yet. Is it worth watching?
I've seen a bit of it. What did you think?
No, but I'd like to. What's it about?

prompts.heard: We were just about to get food. Want to come?
suggestions: I'd like that, thanks.
Maybe next time, but thanks for asking.
Sure. Where were you thinking?

listeningTips: Listen for a moment first to catch the topic.
Nodding and smiling shows you are engaged.
You can leave a conversation any time you like.

scenarios.title: Keeping a conversation going
scenarios.description: The conversation has started and you would like it to continue naturally.
conversationStarters: How has your week been so far?
Do you have any plans coming up?
What do you usually do to unwind?
followUpQuestions: What was that like?
How did that come about?
What happened next?

prompts.heard: It's been busy, to be honest.
suggestions: Same here. What's kept you busy?
That sounds like a lot. Anything good in it?
I know the feeling. Anything you're looking forward to?

prompts.heard: I went hiking at the weekend.
suggestions: That sounds nice. Where did you go?
I'd like to try that. Is it easy to get started?
How was it?

prompts.heard: Yeah, it was fine.
suggestions: What was the best part?
Fine is good. Anything you'd change?
Glad to hear it. What's next?

listeningTips: Short answers are normal. A gentle open question can help.
Pick up on one detail they mention and ask about it.
Comfortable silences are allowed.

scenarios.title: Asking follow-up questions
scenarios.description: You want to show interest by asking a question that builds on what someone just said.
scenarios.setting: A chat with a colleague, classmate or friend
conversationStarters: What made you choose that?
How did you find out about it?
What's the best part so far?
followUpQuestions: Could you tell me more about that?
What was that like for you?
What would you do differently?

prompts.heard: I just started learning guitar.
suggestions: That's great. What made you want to start?
How is it going so far?
What kind of music do you want to play?

prompts.heard: I moved here last month.
suggestions: How are you finding it so far?
What do you like most about it?
What helped you settle in?

prompts.heard: I've been working on a big project.
suggestions: What's it about?
What's the hardest part?
How do you feel it's going?

listeningTips: Listen for a detail you can ask about.
Open questions starting with what or how invite longer answers.
It is fine to say: that sounds interesting.

scenarios.title: Giving and receiving compliments
scenarios.description: You would like to give a genuine compliment or accept one without feeling awkward.
conversationStarters: I really liked how you explained that.
That's a great idea. Thank you for sharing it.
I like your [thing]. Where did you find it?
followUpQuestions: How did you come up with that?
What got you into that?
How long did that take you?

prompts.heard: Thanks, I appreciate that!
suggestions: You're welcome. I meant it.
Happy to say it.
It really helped me.

prompts.heard: You did really well today.
suggestions: Thank you, that means a lot.
Thanks! I put some effort into it.
Thank you. I appreciate you noticing.

prompts.heard: Oh, this old thing?
suggestions: It suits you, in my opinion.
I really do like it.
Fair enough. I just thought I'd say.

listeningTips: Be specific and honest. Specific compliments feel genuine.
When receiving one, a simple thank you is enough.
You do not have to return a compliment.

scenarios.title: Politely disagreeing
scenarios.description: You see something differently and want to say so respectfully.
scenarios.setting: A meeting, class or group chat
conversationStarters: I see it a bit differently. Can I share my view?
That's one way to look at it. Another could be...
I'm not sure I agree. Here's what I think...
followUpQuestions: What led you to that view?
Can you say more about that?
What would change your mind?

prompts.heard: I think we should do it this way.
suggestions: Thanks. I was thinking about it another way. Could I explain?
That's an option. What about the risk of...?
I can see why. I would lean toward...

prompts.heard: You're wrong about that.
suggestions: I see it differently, but I'd like to understand your view.
Maybe we see it differently. Can we look at the facts?
I hear you. Let's agree to disagree on that one.

prompts.heard: Everyone else agrees with this.
suggestions: That may be so. I'd still like to share a different thought.
I appreciate that. Mine is a little different.
Understood. Can I add one point?

listeningTips: Disagreeing about an idea is not disagreeing about the person.
Acknowledge their point first, then share yours.
You can pause and say: let me think about that.

scenarios.title: Setting boundaries
scenarios.description: You want to say no, or limit something, in a calm and kind way.
conversationStarters: I'd like to, but I can't this time.
I'm not comfortable with that, thanks.
I need some time to think. Can I get back to you?
followUpQuestions: Could we do it another way?
Is there a different day that works?
What's the most important part for you?

prompts.heard: Can you cover my shift this weekend?
suggestions: I can't this time, sorry.
I'm not able to this weekend. Could we try next week?
Let me check and get back to you.

prompts.heard: Come on, just stay a bit longer.
suggestions: Thanks, but I'm heading off now.
I'd rather go. Thanks for the invite.
I'm tired. I'll see you next time.

prompts.heard: Why not? It's no big deal.
suggestions: It's just not for me, and that's okay.
I'd rather not say, but I appreciate you asking.
I've decided, thank you.

listeningTips: You do not need to over-explain a no.
A calm, friendly tone and a short sentence are enough.
Other people may feel disappointed. That does not mean you did something wrong.

scenarios.title: Speaking in a meeting
scenarios.description: You want to contribute one idea or question in a meeting or class.
scenarios.setting: A meeting, class or video call
conversationStarters: Can I add something?
I have a question about that.
One idea I had was...
followUpQuestions: Does that make sense?
What do others think?
Could we try that first?

prompts.heard: Does anyone have any thoughts?
suggestions: I have a quick idea, if that's okay.
I'd like to ask about the timeline.
Could I add one point?

prompts.heard: Can you repeat that? I didn't catch it.
suggestions: Of course. In short...
Sure. The main point is...
Let me say that another way.

prompts.heard: Any questions before we finish?
suggestions: Yes. Could we clarify who is doing what?
Just one. When is the next step due?
No, but thank you. That was clear.

listeningTips: Write your point down first if that helps.
One clear sentence is enough.
Questions are a valuable contribution too.

scenarios.title: Handling an awkward pause
scenarios.description: The conversation goes quiet and you are not sure what to do.
conversationStarters: Anything interesting coming up for you this week?
Sorry, I lost my train of thought for a second.
I was just thinking about [topic].
followUpQuestions: What's been the best part of your day?
Have you watched or read anything good lately?
What are you looking forward to?

prompts.heard: (silence for a few seconds)
suggestions: Take a slow breath, then ask: Anything fun planned this week?
That's okay. I'll just take a moment to think.
Smile, and say: Quiet moments are fine by me.

prompts.heard: Um... so... yeah.
suggestions: Yeah, it happens. How's your week going?
No rush. I'm happy to chat about anything.
Let's try a different topic. What are you into lately?

prompts.heard: Sorry, I ran out of things to say!
suggestions: Me too sometimes. It's fine.
No need to be sorry. It's a normal part of chatting.
That's okay. Shall we get a drink?

listeningTips: Pauses feel longer to you than to the other person.
One slow breath can give you time to think.
You can simply say: let me think for a second.
